sourceNote: Descriptions and 'gotcha' facts were written from AWS's own public service overview pages, service FAQs, and the AWS Well-Architected Framework whitepaper. No exam-dump material was used.

services.name: Amazon EC2
services.purpose: provides resizable virtual servers (instances) that you launch, patch and manage yourself
useCases: run a traditional application that needs OS-level access
host workloads that require a specific kernel, agent or licence
lift-and-shift an on-premises virtual machine
facts: You are responsible for patching the guest operating system on EC2 — AWS patches only the hypervisor and below.
Spot Instances can be reclaimed by AWS with a two-minute warning, so they suit fault-tolerant and interruptible work.
Stopping an instance releases its public IPv4 address unless you have attached an Elastic IP.
myths: EC2 instances automatically scale up when CPU rises — scaling requires an Auto Scaling group, it is not built into the instance.
Instance store volumes survive a stop/start — they do not; instance store data is lost when the instance stops or terminates.

services.name: AWS Lambda
services.purpose: runs your code in response to events without you provisioning or managing any servers
useCases: respond to an S3 upload or a DynamoDB stream record
back an API Gateway endpoint
run short scheduled jobs on an EventBridge rule
facts: Lambda bills on requests and on the duration your code actually runs, so idle functions cost nothing.
Memory is the only performance dial you set — CPU and network throughput scale in proportion to the memory you allocate.
A function has a maximum execution timeout of 15 minutes, which rules it out for long batch jobs.
myths: Lambda can run any workload regardless of length — anything over 15 minutes must move to Fargate, ECS, Batch or EC2.
Lambda functions keep local disk state between invocations — /tmp may be reused on a warm start but must never be relied on.

services.name: Amazon ECS
services.purpose: is AWS's own container orchestrator for running and scaling Docker containers
useCases: run containerised microservices without operating a control plane
schedule batch containers behind a load balancer
facts: ECS offers two launch types: EC2, where you manage the container hosts, and Fargate, where AWS does.
ECS has no control-plane charge — you pay only for the EC2 or Fargate capacity that runs your tasks.
myths: ECS requires Kubernetes knowledge — it uses its own task and service model, not Kubernetes objects.
pricing: Pay for underlying EC2 or Fargate capacity

services.name: Amazon EKS
services.purpose: runs upstream-conformant Kubernetes with the control plane managed by AWS
useCases: run existing Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts on AWS
keep workloads portable across clouds and on-premises
facts: Unlike ECS, EKS charges an hourly fee per cluster for the managed control plane, on top of the worker capacity.
EKS worker nodes can be EC2 managed node groups, self-managed nodes, or Fargate profiles.
myths: EKS manages your worker nodes' patching for you — only the control plane is managed unless you use Fargate.

services.name: AWS Fargate
services.purpose: is the serverless compute engine that runs ECS tasks or EKS pods without you managing EC2 instances
useCases: run containers with no host fleet to patch or right-size
spiky container workloads where idle instances would be wasteful
facts: Fargate bills per vCPU-second and GB-second requested by the task, not per instance-hour.
Fargate is not a standalone service — it is a launch type used by ECS and EKS.
myths: You can SSH into a Fargate task's host — there is no host to reach; use ECS Exec for a shell inside the container.

services.name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
services.purpose: deploys and scales a web application from your uploaded code while provisioning the underlying resources for you
useCases: get a standard web app running quickly without hand-building the stack
give developers a paved path onto EC2 and load balancers
facts: Beanstalk itself is free — you pay only for the EC2, load balancer and other resources it creates.
The resources Beanstalk creates remain fully visible and editable in your account, unlike a black-box platform.
myths: Beanstalk is serverless — it provisions real EC2 instances that you can see and are billed for.
pricing: No charge for the service; pay for provisioned resources

services.name: Amazon Lightsail
services.purpose: bundles a virtual server, storage and networking into a fixed monthly price for simple workloads
useCases: run a small website, blog or dev environment at a predictable price
let a newcomer launch a stack without learning VPC design
facts: Lightsail uses a flat monthly bundle price that includes a data-transfer allowance, unlike EC2's metered pricing.
myths: Lightsail is the right choice for large production architectures — it deliberately trades flexibility for simplicity.

services.name: AWS Batch
services.purpose: schedules and runs batch computing jobs, provisioning the right amount of compute for the queue
useCases: run large scientific or financial simulations
process a queue of long-running jobs on Spot capacity
facts: Batch has no additional charge; you pay for the EC2 or Fargate resources it launches to run jobs.
myths: Batch is a scheduler for cron-style tasks — for time-based triggers use EventBridge Scheduler instead.

services.name: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
services.purpose: keeps a group of EC2 instances at the right size, replacing unhealthy instances and scaling on demand
useCases: hold capacity steady by replacing failed instances
scale out on a CloudWatch alarm and back in when load drops
facts: Auto Scaling groups span multiple Availability Zones, which is what makes an EC2 tier resilient to an AZ failure.
There is no charge for Auto Scaling itself — you pay only for the instances it launches.
myths: Auto Scaling makes an instance bigger under load — it adds and removes instances (horizontal scaling), it does not resize them.
An Auto Scaling group distributes traffic — that is the load balancer's job; the group only manages instance count and health.

services.name: AWS Outposts
services.purpose: puts AWS-managed racks of AWS infrastructure in your own data centre, using the same APIs
useCases: keep workloads on-premises for data residency or single-digit-millisecond latency
run a hybrid architecture with one control plane
facts: Outposts hardware is owned, delivered, installed and maintained by AWS but physically lives in your facility.
myths: Outposts is a software product you install on your own servers — it is specific AWS-supplied hardware.
pricing: Per-rack or per-server subscription (1 or 3 year)

services.name: AWS Local Zones
services.purpose: places compute and storage closer to large population centres for latency-sensitive applications
useCases: real-time gaming or media rendering near end users
keep single-digit-millisecond latency to a metro area
facts: A Local Zone is an extension of a parent Region — you enable it, then launch subnets into it from that Region's VPC.
myths: Local Zones are separate Regions with their own account and console — they are extensions of an existing Region.
pricing: Per-resource, similar to the parent Region

services.name: AWS Wavelength
services.purpose: runs AWS compute inside telecom providers' 5G networks for ultra-low-latency mobile applications
useCases: AR/VR delivered to mobile devices
connected-vehicle and IoT workloads needing minimal round trips
facts: Traffic from 5G devices to a Wavelength Zone never leaves the carrier network, which is what removes the latency.
myths: Wavelength is a content delivery network — that is CloudFront; Wavelength runs your compute at the carrier edge.

services.name: Amazon S3
services.purpose: stores any amount of data as objects in buckets, reachable over HTTPS APIs
useCases: host static website assets and media
build a data lake for analytics
store backups and log archives
facts: S3 is object storage — you cannot mount a bucket as a block device or a file system for an operating system.
S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability by storing objects across multiple Availability Zones.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically for a small monitoring fee, with no retrieval charges.
myths: S3 buckets are public by default — new buckets block public access by default and must be explicitly opened.
S3 One Zone-IA is as resilient as S3 Standard — it stores data in a single Availability Zone and is lost if that AZ is destroyed.
pricing: Per GB stored per storage class

services.name: Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes
services.purpose: archives data at very low cost in exchange for slower and charged retrieval
useCases: keep regulatory records for years at minimum cost
long-term retention of backups that are rarely read
facts: Glacier Instant Retrieval reads in milliseconds; Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours; Deep Archive takes up to 12 hours.
Archive classes carry minimum storage durations — deleting early still incurs the remainder of that minimum.
myths: Glacier is a separate service from S3 — the archive tiers are S3 storage classes applied to objects in a bucket.
pricing: Retrieval fee per GB and per request

services.name: Amazon EBS
services.purpose: provides network-attached block volumes that behave like a hard disk for a single EC2 instance
useCases: boot volume for an EC2 instance
the data disk under a self-managed database
facts: An EBS volume lives in one Availability Zone and can only attach to instances in that same AZ.
EBS snapshots are stored in S3 and are incremental — only changed blocks are stored after the first snapshot.
gp3 lets you set IOPS and throughput independently of volume size, which gp2 could not.
myths: EBS can be shared by many instances like a file share — only Multi-Attach io1/io2 volumes attach to several instances, and only within one AZ; for shared file access use EFS.
EBS volumes are backed up automatically — you must schedule snapshots, for example with AWS Backup or Data Lifecycle Manager.

services.name: Amazon EFS
services.purpose: provides an elastic NFS file system that many Linux instances can mount at the same time
useCases: shared content root for a fleet of web servers
home directories or shared scratch space across instances
facts: EFS grows and shrinks automatically as you add and remove files; there is no size to provision.
EFS is regional — mount targets in multiple Availability Zones let instances across AZs use the same file system.
myths: EFS works with Windows instances — EFS is NFS and targets Linux; for SMB/Windows use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
EFS is cheaper than EBS per GB — it is generally more expensive per GB; you pay for shared access and elasticity.

services.name: Amazon FSx
services.purpose: runs fully managed third-party file systems such as Windows File Server, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS
useCases: SMB file shares for Windows workloads with Active Directory integration
high-performance Lustre scratch storage for HPC and ML training
facts: FSx for Windows File Server speaks SMB and integrates with Active Directory, which EFS cannot do.
FSx for Lustre can present an S3 bucket as a file system and lazily load objects as they are read.
myths: FSx is one file system with options — it is a family of distinct file systems with very different characteristics.

services.name: AWS Storage Gateway
services.purpose: gives on-premises applications local access to storage that is actually backed by AWS
useCases: replace a physical tape library with a virtual one backed by S3 Glacier
cache frequently used files locally while storing everything in S3
facts: Gateway types are File Gateway (NFS/SMB to S3), Volume Gateway (iSCSI blocks) and Tape Gateway (virtual tape library).
myths: Storage Gateway moves data one way only — it provides ongoing hybrid access, not a one-off transfer.

services.name: AWS Backup
services.purpose: centralises backup policy, scheduling and retention across many AWS services from one place
useCases: apply one retention policy across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS and FSx
prove backup compliance across an organisation
facts: Backup Vault Lock can make backups immutable so that even an administrator cannot delete them before their retention expires.
AWS Backup can copy backups to another Region or another account for disaster recovery.
myths: AWS Backup protects every AWS service — supported services are an explicit list; check it before relying on it.

services.name: AWS Snow Family
services.purpose: ships physical devices to move very large data sets into AWS when the network would be too slow
useCases: move petabytes out of a data centre with limited bandwidth
collect and pre-process data in a disconnected or harsh location
facts: Data on Snow devices is encrypted with KMS keys and the device is tamper-evident in transit.
myths: Snow devices are the fastest option for any large transfer — for a well-connected site, DataSync or Direct Connect is usually faster end to end.
pricing: Per job and per day of device use

services.name: AWS DataSync
services.purpose: moves large amounts of data over the network between on-premises storage and AWS storage services
useCases: one-off migration of an NFS or SMB share into S3 or EFS
recurring replication of a file server into AWS
facts: DataSync handles encryption in transit, integrity verification and retries automatically, which a plain script would not.
myths: DataSync gives applications live access to AWS storage — that is Storage Gateway; DataSync is a transfer service.

services.name: Amazon RDS
services.purpose: runs managed relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2) with patching and backups handled
useCases: move a self-managed relational database off EC2
run a transactional application store with automated backups
facts: Multi-AZ is for high availability: the standby is a synchronous replica you cannot read from and it fails over automatically.
Read replicas are for scaling reads and use asynchronous replication, so they can lag behind the primary.
You still choose and pay for the instance class and storage — RDS is managed, not serverless, unless you use Aurora Serverless.
myths: A Multi-AZ standby can serve read traffic to spread load — it cannot; use read replicas for that.
RDS lets you connect to the underlying operating system — you get database access only, not shell access.
pricing: Backup storage beyond the free allowance

services.name: Amazon Aurora
services.purpose: is AWS's MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible relational engine with a distributed, self-healing storage layer
useCases: a relational workload needing higher throughput than stock MySQL or PostgreSQL
fast failover and low-lag read scaling
facts: Aurora keeps six copies of your data across three Availability Zones and repairs damaged blocks automatically.
Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity in fine-grained increments in response to load.
Aurora storage grows automatically up to its maximum — you do not provision volume size.
myths: Aurora is a fork of MySQL only — it has both MySQL-compatible and PostgreSQL-compatible editions.
pricing: Instance hours or Aurora Capacity Units

services.name: Amazon DynamoDB
services.purpose: is a serverless key-value and document database delivering single-digit-millisecond reads at any scale
useCases: session, cart and user-profile stores
high-write telemetry and event stores
serverless application back ends
facts: DynamoDB replicates every write across three Availability Zones inside a Region with no configuration from you.
On-demand capacity charges per request with no capacity planning; provisioned capacity is cheaper for steady, predictable traffic.
Global Tables give multi-Region, multi-active replication of a table.
myths: DynamoDB supports SQL joins across tables — it does not; access patterns must be designed into the key schema and indexes.
DAX is built in — DynamoDB Accelerator is a separate cluster you provision when you need microsecond cached reads.

services.name: Amazon ElastiCache
services.purpose: runs managed in-memory Redis OSS/Valkey or Memcached caches in front of slower data stores
useCases: cache expensive database query results
hold session state outside the application servers
leaderboards and rate counters
facts: Redis-compatible ElastiCache supports replication, snapshots and failover; Memcached is a simpler, purely ephemeral cache.
Caching is a common first fix when a read-heavy database is the bottleneck, before scaling the database itself.
myths: ElastiCache persists data durably like a database — treat it as a cache; nodes can be replaced and data lost.

services.name: Amazon MemoryDB
services.purpose: is a Redis-compatible in-memory database that is durable enough to be a primary data store
useCases: microservices that need in-memory speed but cannot lose writes
replace a cache plus separate database pairing
facts: MemoryDB writes to a multi-AZ transaction log, which is what makes it durable where ElastiCache is not.
myths: MemoryDB and ElastiCache are interchangeable — MemoryDB is priced and designed as a durable primary store.

services.name: Amazon Redshift
services.purpose: is a petabyte-scale columnar data warehouse for complex analytic SQL over large data sets
useCases: business-intelligence reporting over years of history
joining and aggregating billions of rows for dashboards
facts: Redshift is built for analytical (OLAP) queries; it is a poor fit for high-concurrency transactional (OLTP) workloads.
Redshift Spectrum queries data left in S3 without loading it into the cluster first.
myths: Redshift is a drop-in replacement for RDS — its columnar design serves reporting, not per-row transactions.

services.name: Amazon DocumentDB
services.purpose: runs a managed document database with MongoDB compatibility
useCases: move a MongoDB workload to a managed service
content catalogues and user profiles stored as JSON documents
facts: Storage scales automatically in 10 GB increments and is replicated six ways across three Availability Zones.
myths: DocumentDB is MongoDB — it is compatible with the MongoDB API, not the same engine, so some features differ.

services.name: Amazon Neptune
services.purpose: is a managed graph database for highly connected data
useCases: fraud-ring detection
recommendation engines
knowledge graphs and network topology
facts: Neptune supports the property-graph query languages Gremlin and openCypher as well as SPARQL for RDF.
myths: A graph database is just a relational database with more joins — Neptune stores relationships as first-class data for traversal speed.

services.name: Amazon Keyspaces
services.purpose: is a serverless, Apache Cassandra-compatible wide-column database
useCases: migrate a Cassandra workload without managing a ring
high-write time-series and device data
facts: Keyspaces is serverless — there are no nodes to size, and tables scale capacity up and down on their own.
myths: Keyspaces requires you to manage Cassandra nodes — it removes the cluster entirely.

services.name: Amazon Timestream
services.purpose: is a purpose-built time-series database with automatic tiering from memory to cost-optimised storage
useCases: IoT sensor telemetry
application and infrastructure metrics kept for long analysis windows
facts: Timestream automatically moves older data from the in-memory store to the magnetic store based on your retention policy.
myths: Any relational table with a timestamp column is equivalent — time-series engines index and compress on time specifically.

services.name: AWS Database Migration Service
services.purpose: migrates databases into AWS with the source staying online during the move
useCases: move an on-premises Oracle database into RDS or Aurora
continuously replicate a database into a data lake
facts: DMS supports homogeneous moves (Oracle to Oracle) and heterogeneous moves when paired with the Schema Conversion Tool.
Change data capture lets DMS keep replicating after the initial full load, which is how cutover downtime stays short.
myths: DMS converts application code and stored procedures — it moves data; schema and code conversion is the Schema Conversion Tool's job.

services.name: Amazon VPC
services.purpose: is your logically isolated private network in AWS where you control subnets, routing and gateways
useCases: separate public web tiers from private application and database tiers
connect to an on-premises network privately
facts: A subnet lives in exactly one Availability Zone, so multi-AZ resilience means multiple subnets.
A subnet is 'public' only because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway — there is no public checkbox.
VPC Flow Logs record accepted and rejected traffic metadata, not packet contents.
myths: Security groups and network ACLs work the same way — security groups are stateful and attach to resources; network ACLs are stateless and attach to subnets.
You can change a VPC's primary CIDR block after creation — you cannot; you can only add secondary CIDRs.
pricing: No charge for the VPC itself
NAT gateways, endpoints and data transfer are charged

services.name: NAT Gateway
services.purpose: lets instances in a private subnet reach the internet for outbound traffic without being reachable from it
useCases: let private application servers download patches and call external APIs
facts: A NAT gateway is zonal — for resilience you deploy one per Availability Zone with matching route tables.
NAT gateways charge an hourly rate plus a per-GB processing charge, which makes them a frequent surprise on bills.
myths: A NAT gateway allows inbound connections from the internet — it only allows responses to outbound connections.

services.name: VPC endpoints
services.purpose: let resources in a VPC reach AWS services privately, without the traffic crossing the internet
useCases: reach S3 from a private subnet without a NAT gateway
keep API traffic to AWS services off the public internet
facts: Gateway endpoints exist for S3 and DynamoDB, are free, and work by adding a route table prefix-list entry.
Interface endpoints are elastic network interfaces powered by PrivateLink and are charged per hour and per GB.
myths: All VPC endpoints cost the same — gateway endpoints are free, interface endpoints are not.
pricing: Interface endpoints per hour and per GB

services.name: AWS PrivateLink
services.purpose: exposes a service privately inside a VPC through an elastic network interface, with no internet gateway or peering
useCases: let a customer VPC consume your SaaS service privately
reach a partner service without opening public routes
facts: PrivateLink connections are one-directional: the consumer initiates to the provider's endpoint service.
myths: PrivateLink is the same as VPC peering — peering joins whole address spaces, PrivateLink exposes a single service endpoint.

services.name: AWS Transit Gateway
services.purpose: acts as a regional hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks through one attachment each
useCases: replace a mesh of VPC peering connections
give hundreds of VPCs shared access to an on-premises network
facts: Transit Gateway removes the n-squared growth of peering connections by giving every network one attachment to a hub.
myths: VPC peering is transitive if you chain it — it is not; that limitation is exactly why Transit Gateway exists.

services.name: AWS Direct Connect
services.purpose: provides a dedicated private network link between your premises and AWS
useCases: consistent low-latency bandwidth for hybrid workloads
large steady data transfer at lower per-GB cost than the internet
facts: Direct Connect offers consistent bandwidth and latency because the traffic never traverses the public internet.
A single Direct Connect connection is not highly available — resilience needs a second connection or a VPN backup.
myths: Direct Connect is encrypted by default — it is private but not encrypted; run a VPN or application-level encryption over it if required.

services.name: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
services.purpose: creates an encrypted IPsec tunnel from your network to AWS over the public internet
useCases: connect a branch office to a VPC quickly
act as a backup path for a Direct Connect link
facts: Each Site-to-Site VPN connection is delivered as two tunnels to two endpoints for redundancy.
myths: A VPN gives the same predictable performance as Direct Connect — it rides the public internet, so latency varies.

services.name: Elastic Load Balancing
services.purpose: distributes incoming traffic across healthy targets in multiple Availability Zones
useCases: spread HTTP traffic across a web fleet
terminate TLS in front of application servers
route by path or hostname to different services
facts: Application Load Balancer works at layer 7 and can route on host, path, header and query string.
Network Load Balancer works at layer 4, handles millions of requests per second and can give you a static IP per AZ.
The load balancer's health checks are what stop traffic reaching a failed instance.
myths: A load balancer scales your fleet — it only distributes traffic; adding capacity is the Auto Scaling group's job.
An Application Load Balancer can balance UDP traffic — it cannot; use a Network Load Balancer.

services.name: Amazon Route 53
services.purpose: is AWS's DNS service, with health checks and traffic-routing policies as well as domain registration
useCases: fail traffic over to a second Region on a health-check failure
route users to the nearest endpoint by latency or geography
facts: Routing policies include simple, weighted, latency-based, failover, geolocation, geoproximity and multivalue answer.
Alias records point at AWS resources such as CloudFront or an ALB and, unlike CNAMEs, work at the zone apex and cost nothing to query.
myths: Route 53 load balances requests — it answers DNS queries; the client then connects directly to whatever address it received.

services.name: Amazon CloudFront
services.purpose: is AWS's content delivery network, caching and serving content from hundreds of edge locations
useCases: speed up a global website or video delivery
reduce origin load and egress cost
put WAF and TLS in front of an origin
facts: CloudFront can front S3, an ALB, EC2 or any HTTP origin — including origins outside AWS.
Origin Access Control lets a bucket serve CloudFront only, so users cannot bypass the CDN by hitting S3 directly.
Data transfer out through CloudFront is usually cheaper than transferring the same bytes directly from the origin.
myths: CloudFront only works with S3 — any reachable HTTP origin works.
CloudFront caches everything automatically — cache behaviour depends on TTLs and the headers, cookies and query strings you tell it to consider.

services.name: AWS Global Accelerator
services.purpose: gives you static anycast IP addresses and routes user traffic onto the AWS backbone at the nearest edge
useCases: improve latency and failover for non-HTTP applications such as gaming or VoIP
provide fixed IPs in front of regional endpoints
facts: Global Accelerator improves network path quality; it does not cache content the way CloudFront does.
myths: Global Accelerator is a CDN — it accelerates and fails over TCP/UDP traffic but stores no cached copies.

services.name: Amazon API Gateway
services.purpose: creates, publishes and secures REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs in front of your back ends
useCases: expose Lambda functions as an HTTP API
apply throttling, API keys and authorisation in one place
version and stage APIs
facts: API Gateway can throttle and cache requests, and enforce authorisation with IAM, Cognito or a Lambda authorizer.
HTTP APIs are cheaper and lower-latency than REST APIs but support fewer features.
myths: API Gateway requires Lambda behind it — it can front any HTTP endpoint, an ALB, or AWS service integrations directly.

services.name: AWS Network Firewall
services.purpose: is a managed stateful network firewall and intrusion prevention service for VPC traffic
useCases: filter outbound traffic by domain name
apply Suricata-compatible intrusion prevention rules at the VPC edge
facts: Network Firewall inspects traffic at the VPC level, which security groups and network ACLs cannot do with deep rules.
myths: AWS WAF and Network Firewall overlap — WAF inspects HTTP(S) requests at the application layer; Network Firewall inspects network traffic.

services.name: AWS IAM
services.purpose: controls who is authenticated and what they are authorised to do in your AWS account
useCases: give an EC2 instance permission to read one S3 bucket via a role
enforce MFA and least privilege for human users
facts: IAM is a global service — users, groups, roles and policies are not tied to a Region.
An explicit Deny in any applicable policy always wins over any Allow.
Roles provide temporary credentials, which is why applications should assume roles rather than embed access keys.
myths: IAM is free but limited by cost — IAM itself has no charge at all.
The root user is just the first IAM user — it is a separate identity that cannot be restricted by IAM policies and should be locked away with MFA.

services.name: AWS IAM Identity Center
services.purpose: centrally manages workforce sign-in and permissions across many AWS accounts and applications
useCases: single sign-on to every account in an organisation
connect an existing identity provider such as Entra ID or Okta
facts: Identity Center assigns permission sets to users for specific accounts, which is how you avoid creating IAM users per account.
myths: Identity Center replaces IAM — it sits on top of IAM and still relies on IAM roles inside each account.

services.name: AWS Organizations
services.purpose: groups multiple AWS accounts under one management account for governance and consolidated billing
useCases: apply guardrails across every account
get one bill and share volume discounts across accounts
facts: Service control policies set the maximum permissions an account can ever use — they never grant permissions on their own.
Consolidated billing pools usage across accounts, so volume tiers and Reserved Instance discounts apply across the organisation.
myths: A service control policy can give a user access they do not already have — it can only restrict what IAM already allows.

services.name: Amazon Cognito
services.purpose: handles sign-up, sign-in and access control for your application's end users
useCases: add social or SAML login to a web or mobile app
exchange a login for temporary AWS credentials
facts: User pools authenticate users and issue tokens; identity pools exchange tokens for temporary AWS credentials.
myths: Cognito manages your staff's access to the AWS console — that is IAM Identity Center; Cognito is for application end users.
pricing: Per monthly active user, with a free tier

services.name: AWS KMS
services.purpose: creates and controls the encryption keys that AWS services use to encrypt your data
useCases: encrypt S3 objects, EBS volumes and RDS databases with a key you control
audit every use of a key through CloudTrail
facts: AWS managed keys are created and rotated for you; customer managed keys let you set the policy, rotation and grants.
KMS keys are regional — you cannot use a key from one Region to decrypt data in another.
Every KMS API call is logged to CloudTrail, giving an audit trail of who decrypted what.
myths: KMS stores your data — it stores and controls keys; your data stays in the service that encrypted it.
pricing: Per customer managed key per month

services.name: AWS CloudHSM
services.purpose: gives you dedicated, FIPS 140-3 validated hardware security modules that only you can access
useCases: meet a regulation that requires single-tenant key hardware
offload TLS or run a private certificate authority
facts: With CloudHSM you control the keys entirely — AWS cannot recover them if you lose your credentials.
myths: CloudHSM is just a more expensive KMS — it is single-tenant hardware with no AWS access to the key material.

services.name: AWS Secrets Manager
services.purpose: stores, encrypts and automatically rotates secrets such as database credentials and API keys
useCases: rotate an RDS password on a schedule with no code change
keep credentials out of source control and environment variables
facts: Built-in rotation with Lambda is the main thing Secrets Manager offers over Systems Manager Parameter Store.
myths: Parameter Store and Secrets Manager are identical — Parameter Store is free for standard parameters but does not rotate secrets for you.

services.name: AWS Certificate Manager
services.purpose: provisions, manages and renews TLS certificates for AWS services
useCases: put a free public certificate on an ALB, CloudFront distribution or API Gateway
facts: Public certificates issued by ACM are free and renew automatically as long as validation stays in place.
A certificate used by CloudFront must be requested in the us-east-1 Region regardless of where your origin is.
myths: ACM certificates can be exported and installed on your own EC2 web server — public ACM certificates cannot be exported.

services.name: AWS WAF
services.purpose: filters HTTP and HTTPS requests before they reach your application, by rule
useCases: block SQL injection and cross-site scripting patterns
rate-limit a noisy IP address
geo-block regions
facts: WAF attaches to CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, API Gateway, AppSync or Cognito user pools — not directly to EC2.
myths: WAF stops volumetric network floods — that is Shield's job; WAF inspects application-layer requests.

services.name: AWS Shield
services.purpose: protects AWS-hosted applications against distributed denial-of-service attacks
useCases: absorb volumetric network floods
get 24/7 response-team support during an attack (Advanced)
facts: Shield Standard is enabled for every AWS customer at no extra cost.
Shield Advanced adds cost protection for scaling charges during an attack and access to the Shield Response Team.
myths: You must enable Shield Standard — it is already on for every account by default.
pricing: Advanced monthly subscription plus data transfer

services.name: Amazon GuardDuty
services.purpose: continuously analyses account and network telemetry to detect threats using machine learning and threat intelligence
useCases: spot cryptomining, credential compromise or unusual API calls
monitor every account in an organisation from one place
facts: GuardDuty reads CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs directly — you do not have to enable or ship those logs to it.
myths: GuardDuty blocks the attacks it finds — it detects and reports; remediation is up to you or an automation you build.
pricing: Per volume of events and logs analysed

services.name: Amazon Inspector
services.purpose: continuously scans workloads for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure
useCases: find known CVEs in EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions
prioritise patching by real risk score
facts: Inspector scans automatically and continuously as new CVEs are published, not only when you ask it to.
myths: Inspector detects live attacks — that is GuardDuty; Inspector finds vulnerabilities before they are exploited.

services.name: Amazon Macie
services.purpose: discovers and classifies sensitive data such as personal information stored in S3
useCases: find buckets containing credit-card or health data
prove where regulated data lives before an audit
facts: Macie is specific to Amazon S3 — it does not scan EBS volumes, databases or file systems.
myths: Macie scans all your storage services — it is S3-focused.

services.name: AWS Security Hub
services.purpose: aggregates findings from AWS security services into one dashboard and checks them against standards
useCases: one view of GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and partner findings
continuous CIS or AWS Foundational Security Best Practices scoring
facts: Security Hub normalises findings into a common format so tools with different output can be compared and routed.
myths: Security Hub replaces GuardDuty and Inspector — it consumes their findings; it does not detect on its own.

services.name: Amazon Detective
services.purpose: builds linked graphs from your logs so you can investigate the root cause of a security finding
useCases: trace how a compromised credential was used over time
investigate a GuardDuty finding without hand-writing log queries
facts: Detective automatically ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings to build its behaviour graph.
myths: Detective generates findings — it explains findings that other services generated.

services.name: AWS Artifact
services.purpose: is the self-service portal for AWS's compliance reports and agreements
useCases: download the SOC 2 or ISO 27001 report for an auditor
accept a business associate addendum
facts: Artifact is where AWS's own audit evidence lives — it says nothing about whether your workloads are compliant.
myths: Artifact audits your account for compliance — that is Config, Audit Manager and Security Hub; Artifact only serves AWS's documents.

services.name: AWS Resource Access Manager
services.purpose: shares specific resources such as subnets and Transit Gateways with other AWS accounts
useCases: run a shared-VPC model where one account owns the network
share a Transit Gateway or licence configuration organisation-wide
facts: Sharing with RAM avoids duplicating resources per account, which reduces both cost and configuration drift.
myths: RAM copies resources into the other account — the resource stays owned by one account and is used by the others.

services.name: Amazon CloudWatch
services.purpose: collects metrics, logs, traces and alarms so you can see and react to how your systems behave
useCases: alarm when CPU or error rate crosses a threshold
centralise application logs
trigger Auto Scaling from a metric
facts: Memory and disk usage inside an EC2 instance are not collected by default — that needs the CloudWatch agent.
A CloudWatch alarm can trigger Auto Scaling, publish to SNS or run an EC2 action such as reboot.
CloudWatch Logs Insights lets you query log groups with a purpose-built query language.
myths: CloudWatch records who called an AWS API — that is CloudTrail; CloudWatch records what systems are doing.
All CloudWatch metrics are one-minute by default — basic monitoring for EC2 is five-minute; detailed monitoring is charged.
pricing: Per GB of logs ingested and stored

services.name: AWS CloudTrail
services.purpose: records the API calls made in your account: who did what, when, and from where
useCases: investigate who deleted a resource
keep an immutable audit trail for compliance
facts: Management events are recorded for the last 90 days in Event history for free; longer retention needs a trail writing to S3.
Data events, such as individual S3 object reads, are not logged by default and are charged separately.
myths: CloudTrail monitors performance — it audits API activity; CloudWatch handles metrics and logs.
pricing: Data events and additional trails charged

services.name: AWS Config
services.purpose: records resource configuration over time and evaluates it against rules you define
useCases: prove no S3 bucket was public at any point last quarter
auto-remediate resources that drift out of policy
facts: Config keeps a configuration timeline per resource, so you can see exactly what changed and when.
myths: Config records API calls — it records resource state; CloudTrail records the calls that changed it.

services.name: AWS CloudFormation
services.purpose: provisions and updates AWS resources from declarative templates as a single stack
useCases: stand up identical environments for dev, test and production
roll a whole environment back when a deployment fails
facts: A failed stack update rolls back to the previous state by default, which is a major reason to use it over scripts.
Change sets show you what a template update would do before you apply it.
StackSets deploy the same stack across many accounts and Regions at once.
myths: CloudFormation has a charge per stack — the service is free; you pay only for the resources created.

services.name: AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK)
services.purpose: lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Java, Go or C#, which it compiles into CloudFormation
useCases: reuse infrastructure patterns as code constructs
keep infrastructure in the same language as the application
facts: CDK synthesises to a CloudFormation template, so every CDK deployment is ultimately a CloudFormation stack.
myths: CDK is a replacement for CloudFormation — it is a higher-level authoring layer on top of it.

services.name: AWS Systems Manager
services.purpose: gives you operational control of your fleet: patching, run commands, session access and parameter storage
useCases: patch a fleet on a maintenance window
open a shell on an instance without SSH or a bastion
store configuration in Parameter Store
facts: Session Manager gives shell access with no open inbound port, no bastion host and full session logging.
Parameter Store holds configuration and secrets; standard parameters are free.
myths: Systems Manager needs SSH access to work — it uses an outbound-only agent, which is why it removes bastion hosts.
pricing: Advanced parameters and some capabilities charged

services.name: AWS Trusted Advisor
services.purpose: inspects your account and recommends improvements across cost, performance, security, fault tolerance, limits and operations
useCases: find idle resources wasting money
spot security groups open to the world
check service quota headroom
facts: The full set of Trusted Advisor checks requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise Support plan.
myths: Trusted Advisor fixes the problems it finds — it recommends; you or an automation must act.
pricing: Full checks require paid Support plan

services.name: AWS Control Tower
services.purpose: sets up and governs a secure multi-account AWS environment using prescriptive best practices
useCases: stand up a landing zone with logging, audit and guardrail accounts
enforce controls as new accounts are vended
facts: Control Tower builds on Organizations, IAM Identity Center, Config and CloudTrail rather than replacing them.
myths: Control Tower is required for multi-account setups — Organizations alone is enough; Control Tower adds an opinionated landing zone.
pricing: No charge for the service; underlying services charged

services.name: AWS Service Catalog
services.purpose: publishes an approved catalogue of products that users can launch without broad permissions
useCases: let developers self-serve an approved database stack
constrain what sizes and Regions users may deploy
facts: Users launch products through Service Catalog's own permissions, so they never need permission to create the resources directly.
myths: Service Catalog is the AWS Marketplace — Marketplace sells third-party software; Service Catalog publishes your own approved stacks.
pricing: Per API call beyond the free tier

services.name: AWS Health Dashboard
services.purpose: shows AWS service health and events that specifically affect your account's resources
useCases: get notified about scheduled maintenance on your instances
check whether an outage is AWS-side or yours
facts: The account-specific view lists events affecting your own resources, which the public service-status page does not.
myths: The Health Dashboard only shows global outages — the personalised view is resource-specific.

services.name: AWS Compute Optimizer
services.purpose: recommends optimal resource sizes for EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS, Lambda and ECS on Fargate from real usage
useCases: find over-provisioned instances
right-size Lambda memory for cost or speed
facts: Compute Optimizer bases recommendations on observed CloudWatch metrics, so it needs a usage history to be useful.
myths: Compute Optimizer applies its recommendations — it only recommends.

services.name: AWS Well-Architected Tool
services.purpose: guides you through reviewing a workload against the Well-Architected Framework pillars and tracks the improvement plan
useCases: run a structured architecture review
track risks and remediation over time
facts: The tool produces a risk list per pillar; the framework itself is a whitepaper, the tool is the workflow around it.
myths: The Well-Architected Tool scans your account automatically — it is a questionnaire-driven review.

services.name: AWS License Manager
services.purpose: tracks and enforces software licence usage across AWS and on-premises
useCases: stop launching instances once a licence limit is hit
report on bring-your-own-licence usage for an audit
facts: License Manager can hard-stop non-compliant launches, not merely report on them.
myths: License Manager buys licences for you — it tracks and enforces the ones you already hold.

services.name: AWS Cost Explorer
services.purpose: visualises and analyses your AWS spending and usage over time, with forecasts
useCases: find which service or account drove a spike
forecast next month's bill
review Savings Plans recommendations
facts: Cost Explorer can break spend down by tag, which is why a consistent tagging policy matters for cost allocation.
myths: Cost Explorer stops spending — it reports; Budgets alerts and Organizations policies constrain.

services.name: AWS Budgets
services.purpose: sets cost, usage, Reserved Instance and Savings Plans thresholds and alerts you when they are approached or exceeded
useCases: email or SNS alert when monthly spend passes a limit
alert on forecast, before the money is actually spent
facts: Budgets can alert on forecast spend as well as actual spend, which is what gives you time to react.
myths: A budget caps your spending — it notifies; it does not stop resources running unless you wire up a Budget Action.
pricing: Small monthly charge per budget beyond that

services.name: AWS Cost and Usage Report
services.purpose: delivers the most detailed, line-item breakdown of your AWS usage and cost into an S3 bucket
useCases: feed billing data into Athena or QuickSight
do chargeback to internal teams by tag
facts: The report is the authoritative, line-item source — more granular than anything Cost Explorer shows.
myths: The report appears in the console — it is delivered as files to S3 for you to query.
pricing: No charge for the report; S3 storage charged

services.name: AWS Pricing Calculator
services.purpose: estimates the cost of an architecture before you build it
useCases: produce a cost estimate for a proposal
compare two designs on price
facts: The calculator is for estimating future cost; Cost Explorer reports what you have already spent.
myths: The calculator reads your account and prices it — you enter the configuration yourself.

services.name: AWS Marketplace
services.purpose: is a curated catalogue of third-party software you can buy and deploy, billed through your AWS account
useCases: buy a commercial firewall appliance AMI
subscribe to a SaaS product on one consolidated bill
facts: Marketplace purchases appear on your normal AWS bill, which simplifies procurement.
myths: Marketplace software is built and supported by AWS — it is third-party software sold through AWS.
pricing: Varies by product; charged to your AWS bill

services.name: Amazon SQS
services.purpose: is a fully managed message queue that decouples producers from consumers
useCases: buffer bursts of work so the back end is not overwhelmed
let a failed consumer retry without losing the message
facts: SQS is pull-based: consumers poll the queue, and a message stays invisible for the visibility timeout while being processed.
FIFO queues guarantee ordering and exactly-once processing; standard queues offer higher throughput with at-least-once delivery.
A dead-letter queue captures messages that repeatedly fail so they can be inspected instead of lost.
myths: SQS pushes messages to subscribers — that is SNS; SQS consumers poll.
Standard queues preserve order — only FIFO queues do.

services.name: Amazon SNS
services.purpose: is a publish/subscribe service that pushes one message to many subscribers
useCases: fan a single event out to several queues and Lambda functions
send operational alerts by email or SMS
facts: SNS is push-based and delivers to subscribers such as SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTPS endpoints, email and SMS.
The common fan-out pattern is SNS publishing to several SQS queues so each consumer processes independently.
myths: SNS stores messages until a consumer is ready — it delivers immediately; use SQS when you need durable buffering.

services.name: Amazon EventBridge
services.purpose: routes events from AWS services, your applications and SaaS partners to targets based on rules
useCases: react to an AWS service event such as an instance state change
schedule jobs on a cron expression
route SaaS events into your systems
facts: EventBridge rules match on the event's JSON content, so routing logic lives in the bus rather than in your code.
The schema registry and archive/replay features are what set EventBridge apart from plain SNS.
myths: EventBridge is just a renamed CloudWatch Events — it began there but adds custom buses, partner sources, schemas and replay.

services.name: AWS Step Functions
services.purpose: coordinates multiple services into serverless workflows with visual state machines, retries and error handling
useCases: orchestrate a multi-step order pipeline
add retry and catch logic without writing it in every function
facts: Standard workflows are durable for up to a year and are billed per state transition; Express workflows are cheaper for high-volume, short runs.
Step Functions can call over 200 AWS services directly, avoiding glue Lambda functions.
myths: Step Functions replaces Lambda — it orchestrates Lambda and other services; it does not run your business logic itself.

services.name: AWS AppSync
services.purpose: is a managed GraphQL service that combines multiple data sources behind one API, with real-time subscriptions
useCases: give a mobile app one query endpoint over several tables and services
push live updates to connected clients
facts: AppSync resolvers can talk directly to DynamoDB, Aurora, OpenSearch, Lambda and HTTP endpoints.
myths: AppSync is API Gateway for GraphQL — API Gateway can front a GraphQL server, but AppSync adds resolvers, caching and subscriptions natively.
pricing: Per million query and mutation operations

services.name: Amazon MQ
services.purpose: runs managed Apache ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ brokers for applications that need standard messaging protocols
useCases: migrate an existing JMS or AMQP application without rewriting it
facts: Amazon MQ exists mainly for migration: it speaks industry-standard protocols that SQS and SNS do not.
myths: Amazon MQ is the default choice for new AWS applications — for new work SQS/SNS/EventBridge scale better and cost less.

services.name: AWS Amplify
services.purpose: builds, deploys and hosts full-stack web and mobile front ends with a connected AWS back end
useCases: host a React or Next.js site with CI/CD from a Git branch
wire a front end to Cognito, AppSync and S3 quickly
facts: Amplify Hosting builds from your Git repository on push and serves through a managed CDN.
myths: Amplify is only a hosting service — it also generates and manages back-end resources.

services.name: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
services.purpose: ingests and stores large real-time data streams for multiple consumers to read
useCases: clickstream and telemetry ingestion
let several applications process the same stream independently
facts: Records stay in the stream for a retention period (24 hours by default, up to 365 days), so multiple consumers can replay them.
Throughput scales by shard in provisioned mode, or automatically in on-demand mode.
myths: Kinesis Data Streams delivers straight into S3 or Redshift — that is Firehose; Data Streams is a stream you read from.

services.name: Amazon Data Firehose
services.purpose: delivers streaming data to destinations such as S3, Redshift, OpenSearch and Splunk with no code
useCases: land raw event data in S3 in near real time
buffer, compress and convert records on the way to storage
facts: Firehose is fully managed and near real time — it buffers by size or time before delivering, so it is not sub-second.
myths: Firehose lets several consumers read the same records — it is a delivery pipeline to a destination, not a replayable stream.

services.name: Amazon MSK
services.purpose: runs fully managed Apache Kafka clusters
useCases: move an existing Kafka workload to AWS unchanged
high-throughput event streaming with the Kafka ecosystem
facts: MSK runs real open-source Kafka, so existing Kafka clients, connectors and tooling work as-is.
myths: MSK is Kinesis with a different name — it is genuine Apache Kafka with its own APIs and operational model.

services.name: Amazon Athena
services.purpose: runs standard SQL directly against data in S3 with no infrastructure to manage
useCases: query log or CUR data in place
ad-hoc analysis of a data lake without loading a warehouse
facts: Athena charges per terabyte of data scanned, so partitioning and columnar formats such as Parquet cut cost dramatically.
Athena uses the AWS Glue Data Catalog for table definitions.
myths: Athena copies your data into a database first — it reads directly from S3.

services.name: AWS Glue
services.purpose: is a serverless data integration service providing a data catalog, crawlers and ETL jobs
useCases: crawl S3 and infer table schemas
transform raw data into partitioned Parquet for querying
facts: The Glue Data Catalog is a shared metadata store used by Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum and Lake Formation.
myths: Glue is only an ETL runner — its catalog is arguably its most widely used component.
pricing: Per DPU-hour for jobs and crawlers

services.name: Amazon EMR
services.purpose: runs big-data frameworks such as Spark, Hive and Presto on managed clusters
useCases: large-scale Spark transformations
existing Hadoop workloads moved to AWS
facts: EMR clusters can run task nodes on Spot Instances, which is a major cost lever for tolerant batch work.
myths: EMR is serverless by default — EMR Serverless exists, but classic EMR provisions a real cluster you size.
pricing: EC2 or EKS capacity plus an EMR per-instance surcharge

services.name: AWS Lake Formation
services.purpose: builds and secures a data lake with fine-grained permissions down to table, column and row level
useCases: grant analysts access to some columns but not others
centralise data-lake permissions across accounts
facts: Lake Formation permissions are enforced by the query engines (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR) that read the catalog.
myths: Lake Formation stores your data — the data stays in S3; Lake Formation governs access to it.
pricing: No charge for permissions; underlying services charged

services.name: Amazon OpenSearch Service
services.purpose: runs managed OpenSearch clusters for search, log analytics and vector similarity queries
useCases: full-text search over a product catalogue
centralised log analytics with dashboards
vector store for retrieval-augmented generation
facts: OpenSearch supports k-nearest-neighbour vector search, which is why it appears in generative-AI reference architectures.
myths: OpenSearch is a relational database — it is a search and analytics engine with a different consistency and query model.

services.name: Amazon QuickSight
services.purpose: is a serverless business-intelligence service for dashboards and visualisations
useCases: publish dashboards over Redshift, Athena or S3 data
embed analytics in an application
facts: The SPICE in-memory engine caches data so dashboards stay fast without hitting the source on every view.
myths: QuickSight requires a data warehouse — it can query S3 through Athena, or several other sources directly.
pricing: Per author and per reader per month

services.name: Amazon SageMaker AI
services.purpose: covers the full machine-learning lifecycle: prepare data, train, tune, deploy and monitor models
useCases: train a custom model on your own data
host a real-time inference endpoint
run automated ML pipelines
facts: SageMaker is the build-your-own-model service; Bedrock is the use-someone-else's-foundation-model service.
Real-time endpoints bill for the instance while it exists, so idle endpoints are a common source of waste.
myths: SageMaker is a single tool — it is a family of capabilities (Studio, Training, Endpoints, Pipelines, Feature Store and more).

services.name: Amazon Bedrock
services.purpose: gives API access to foundation models from several providers, plus knowledge bases, agents and guardrails
useCases: add text generation or summarisation to an application
build retrieval-augmented generation over your own documents
facts: Bedrock is serverless — there is no model infrastructure to provision for on-demand inference.
Guardrails apply content filters and topic restrictions independently of which model you use.
Knowledge Bases handle the chunking, embedding and retrieval steps of a RAG pipeline for you.
myths: Bedrock trains models on your prompts — AWS states customer prompts and outputs are not used to train the base models.

services.name: Amazon Rekognition
services.purpose: analyses images and video for objects, scenes, text, faces and unsafe content
useCases: moderate user-uploaded images
detect and index faces in a media library
facts: Rekognition is a pre-trained API — you call it without training a model, though Custom Labels allows your own classes.
myths: Rekognition needs training data before it works — the standard APIs are pre-trained.
pricing: Per image or per minute of video analysed

services.name: Amazon Comprehend
services.purpose: extracts meaning from text: entities, key phrases, sentiment, language and PII
useCases: score support tickets for sentiment
redact personal data from documents
facts: Comprehend can detect and redact personally identifiable information, which is often used as a compliance control.
myths: Comprehend translates text — that is Amazon Translate.

services.name: Amazon Textract
services.purpose: extracts text, forms and tables from scanned documents
useCases: digitise invoices and claim forms
pull structured key-value pairs from PDFs
facts: Textract preserves structure — forms and tables come back as related fields, not one flat blob of text.
myths: Textract is plain OCR — it also understands form and table structure.

services.name: Amazon Transcribe
services.purpose: converts speech in audio and video into text
useCases: subtitle recorded media
transcribe and analyse contact-centre calls
facts: Transcribe supports speaker identification and custom vocabularies for domain-specific terms.
myths: Transcribe reads text aloud — that is Amazon Polly, the opposite direction.

services.name: Amazon Polly
services.purpose: turns text into lifelike speech
useCases: voice responses in an application
audio versions of written articles
facts: Polly can return speech marks describing word timing, which is used to synchronise captions or animation.
myths: Polly transcribes speech — that is Amazon Transcribe.

services.name: Amazon Translate
services.purpose: performs neural machine translation between languages
useCases: localise user-generated content
translate support conversations in real time
facts: Custom terminology lets you force specific translations for brand and product names.
myths: Translate detects sentiment — that is Amazon Comprehend.

services.name: Amazon Lex
services.purpose: builds conversational interfaces — chatbots and voice bots — using intents and slots
useCases: automate common contact-centre questions
add a chat assistant to an application
facts: Lex uses the same automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding technology as Alexa.
myths: Lex is a foundation-model chatbot — it is intent-and-slot based; for open-ended generation use Bedrock.

services.name: Amazon Kendra
services.purpose: provides intelligent enterprise search across your document repositories using natural language
useCases: search across SharePoint, S3 and Confluence from one place
retrieve context for a generative-AI answer
facts: Kendra returns ranked passages and direct answers, which makes it a common retrieval source in RAG architectures.
myths: Kendra is a keyword search index — it interprets natural-language questions rather than matching terms.

services.name: Amazon Q
services.purpose: is a generative-AI assistant that answers questions over your business data and helps developers write and update code
useCases: answer staff questions grounded in internal documents
explain or refactor code in an IDE
facts: Amazon Q comes in variants aimed at business users and at developers, with different data connectors.
myths: Amazon Q is the same product as Bedrock — Bedrock is the model platform you build on; Q is a finished assistant.
pricing: Per user per month by edition

services.name: AWS CodePipeline
services.purpose: models and runs continuous delivery pipelines as a sequence of stages and actions
useCases: build, test and deploy on every commit
add a manual approval gate before production
facts: CodePipeline orchestrates; the actual build and deploy work is done by CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, CloudFormation or third-party actions.
myths: CodePipeline compiles your code — CodeBuild does that.
pricing: Per active pipeline per month, or per action execution

services.name: AWS CodeBuild
services.purpose: compiles source, runs tests and produces deployable artifacts on managed build servers
useCases: run unit tests on every pull request
build container images and push them to ECR
facts: CodeBuild bills per build minute by compute type, so there is no idle build fleet to pay for.
myths: CodeBuild deploys your application — deployment is CodeDeploy's or CloudFormation's job.
pricing: Per build minute by compute type

services.name: AWS CodeDeploy
services.purpose: automates application deployments to EC2, on-premises servers, Lambda and ECS with controlled rollout strategies
useCases: blue/green deployment with automatic rollback on alarm
canary shift of Lambda traffic
facts: CodeDeploy supports in-place, blue/green, canary and linear traffic-shifting strategies with automatic rollback.
myths: CodeDeploy only works on EC2 — it also deploys to Lambda, ECS and on-premises servers.
pricing: Free to EC2/Lambda/ECS; per on-premises instance update

services.name: AWS X-Ray
services.purpose: traces requests as they travel through a distributed application, showing where latency and errors occur
useCases: find which microservice is slow in a chain of calls
visualise a service map of dependencies
facts: X-Ray shows per-request traces across services, which aggregate CloudWatch metrics cannot.
myths: X-Ray replaces CloudWatch Logs — it complements them with request-level tracing.

services.name: AWS CLI
services.purpose: is the command-line tool for controlling AWS services and scripting operations
useCases: script repeatable operational tasks
manage resources from a terminal or CI job
facts: The CLI uses the same public APIs and the same IAM permissions as the console.
myths: The CLI can do less than the console — it typically exposes new API capability before the console does.

services.name: AWS SDKs
services.purpose: are the language-specific libraries that let your application code call AWS APIs
useCases: call S3 or DynamoDB from application code
handle retries, signing and pagination correctly
facts: SDKs implement request signing, retries with backoff and credential resolution so you do not hand-roll them.
myths: You must embed access keys to use an SDK — on AWS compute the SDK picks up role credentials automatically.

services.name: AWS Migration Hub
services.purpose: tracks the progress of application migrations across AWS and partner migration tools in one place
useCases: report migration status to stakeholders
group servers into applications and follow their move
facts: Migration Hub aggregates status from tools such as Application Migration Service and DMS rather than moving data itself.
myths: Migration Hub performs the migration — it tracks migrations performed by other tools.

services.name: AWS Application Migration Service
services.purpose: lifts and shifts physical, virtual and cloud servers onto EC2 with continuous block-level replication
useCases: rehost a data centre onto EC2 with minimal downtime
test a cutover without disrupting the source
facts: Continuous replication means cutover downtime is measured in minutes rather than the length of a full copy.
myths: It refactors applications for the cloud — it rehosts them as-is; modernisation is a separate exercise.
pricing: Per replicating source server per hour, with a free period

concepts.name: Regions and Availability Zones
concepts.purpose: describes how AWS divides the world into Regions, each containing multiple isolated Availability Zones
facts: An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centres with independent power, cooling and networking.
Availability Zones within a Region are close enough for synchronous replication but far enough apart to fail independently.
Deploying across at least two Availability Zones is the baseline for high availability inside one Region.
myths: An Availability Zone is a single data centre — it is one or more.
Data is copied between Regions automatically — cross-Region replication is always something you configure.

concepts.name: Edge locations
concepts.purpose: are the global points of presence used to cache content and terminate connections close to users
facts: Edge locations serve CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator, WAF and Shield, and vastly outnumber Regions.
myths: You launch EC2 instances in edge locations — you do not; edge locations run AWS edge services.

concepts.name: Shared responsibility model
concepts.purpose: divides security duties: AWS secures the cloud itself, you secure what you put in it
facts: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud: hardware, the global infrastructure, and the managed service software.
You are responsible for security IN the cloud: your data, identity and access, OS patching where applicable, and network configuration.
The boundary moves with the service — with Lambda you never patch an OS, with EC2 you always do.
myths: AWS encrypts all your data automatically — you choose and configure encryption for most services.
Moving to managed services removes all your security duties — IAM, data classification and access control stay yours in every service.

concepts.name: AWS Well-Architected Framework pillars
concepts.purpose: gives six pillars for evaluating an architecture
facts: The six pillars are Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability.
Sustainability was added as the sixth pillar in 2021.
myths: There are five pillars — Sustainability made it six.

concepts.name: Advantages of cloud computing
concepts.purpose: are the benefits AWS cites for moving from owned data centres to cloud
facts: Trading capital expense for variable expense means you pay only for what you consume.
Massive economies of scale mean AWS's aggregate buying power produces lower per-unit prices than any one customer could reach.
You stop guessing capacity, gain speed and agility, stop spending money running data centres, and go global in minutes.
myths: Cloud is always cheaper than on-premises — it changes the cost model; steady predictable workloads can be cheaper owned.

concepts.name: Cloud deployment models
concepts.purpose: describes whether a workload runs entirely in the cloud, entirely on-premises, or across both
facts: The three models are cloud-based, on-premises (private cloud), and hybrid, which combines the two.
myths: Hybrid means running two separate systems — it means connecting them, typically with Direct Connect or VPN.

concepts.name: The migration strategies (the 7 Rs)
concepts.purpose: names the standard options for what to do with each application when moving to AWS
facts: The seven are rehost, replatform, refactor, repurchase, retire, retain and relocate.
myths: Rehost and replatform are the same — rehost lifts the server as-is, replatform makes small optimisations such as moving to RDS.

concepts.name: EC2 purchasing options
concepts.purpose: are the ways you can pay for EC2 capacity, each trading flexibility for discount
facts: On-Demand has no commitment and the highest per-hour rate; it suits unpredictable or short workloads.
Reserved Instances and Savings Plans give large discounts for a one- or three-year commitment.
Spot Instances offer the deepest discount but can be interrupted with two minutes' notice.
Dedicated Hosts give you a physical server, which is usually about licensing compliance rather than performance.
myths: Spot Instances are cheaper Reserved Instances — Spot is interruptible spare capacity with no commitment or guarantee.
A Savings Plan locks you to one instance type — Compute Savings Plans apply across instance families, Regions, Lambda and Fargate.

concepts.name: AWS Support plans
concepts.purpose: are the tiers of technical support AWS sells, differing in response time and included services
facts: The tiers are Basic, Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise.
A Technical Account Manager is included with Enterprise On-Ramp (pooled) and Enterprise (designated), not with Business.
Business and above include 24/7 phone, chat and email access to Cloud Support Engineers, plus the full Trusted Advisor check set.
myths: Basic Support includes technical help with your architecture — Basic covers billing and account questions plus service health, not technical troubleshooting.
Developer Support gives you 24/7 phone support — it gives business-hours email access to Cloud Support Associates.

concepts.name: Security groups versus network ACLs
concepts.purpose: distinguishes the two VPC firewall layers that candidates most often confuse
facts: Security groups are stateful: allow traffic in and the response is automatically allowed out.
Network ACLs are stateless: you must write both the inbound and the outbound rule.
Security groups only support allow rules; network ACLs support both allow and deny rules.
myths: Security groups can explicitly deny an IP address — they cannot; use a network ACL or AWS WAF for that.
Network ACLs attach to instances — they attach to subnets.

concepts.name: Horizontal and vertical scaling
concepts.purpose: describes the two directions you can add capacity
facts: Scaling out (horizontal) adds more instances; scaling up (vertical) makes one instance bigger.
Horizontal scaling is what gives both elasticity and fault tolerance, because the work survives one instance failing.
myths: Vertical scaling has no downtime on EC2 — changing instance type requires stopping the instance.

concepts.name: High availability, fault tolerance and disaster recovery
concepts.purpose: separates three commonly conflated resilience goals
facts: High availability minimises downtime, usually across Availability Zones; disaster recovery restores service after a larger failure, usually across Regions.
RPO is how much data you can afford to lose; RTO is how long you can afford to be down.
The four common DR strategies, from cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest, are backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active/active.
myths: Multi-AZ is a disaster recovery strategy — it is high availability within one Region; DR normally implies a second Region.
Backups alone give you a low RTO — restoring large data sets takes time, which is exactly what pilot light and warm standby buy down.

concepts.name: Durability versus availability
concepts.purpose: separates the chance of losing data from the chance of not being able to reach it
facts: Durability is the probability an object survives; availability is the probability you can access it right now. S3 Standard quotes eleven nines of durability and four nines of availability.
myths: Higher durability implies higher availability — S3 One Zone-IA keeps the same durability design but lower availability.

concepts.name: Encryption at rest and in transit
concepts.purpose: distinguishes protecting stored data from protecting data moving over a network
facts: Encryption at rest protects stored data, typically with KMS keys; encryption in transit protects data on the wire, typically with TLS.
Server-side encryption is done by the AWS service; client-side encryption happens in your application before the data is sent.
myths: Enabling encryption at rest also encrypts traffic to the service — they are separate controls.

concepts.name: Least privilege and IAM best practice
concepts.purpose: is the principle of granting only the permissions a task actually needs
facts: Grant permissions to roles and groups rather than to individual users, and prefer temporary credentials over long-lived access keys.
Enable MFA on the root user, remove its access keys, and use it only for the few tasks that require it.
myths: Attaching AdministratorAccess to a role is fine if only a few people can assume it — least privilege applies to the role's permissions, not only to who can assume it.

concepts.name: Infrastructure as code
concepts.purpose: means defining infrastructure in version-controlled templates rather than clicking through a console
facts: Infrastructure as code makes environments reproducible and changes reviewable, and is a core Operational Excellence practice.
myths: Infrastructure as code is only for large teams — reproducibility matters at any size.

concepts.name: Tagging and cost allocation
concepts.purpose: attaches key-value metadata to resources so they can be grouped for cost, automation and access control
facts: Cost allocation tags must be activated in the billing console before they appear in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report.
Tags can drive IAM conditions and automation as well as cost reporting.
myths: Tags apply retroactively to past bills — activated cost allocation tags only affect data from activation onwards.

concepts.name: Service quotas
concepts.purpose: are the per-account, per-Region limits AWS applies to resource counts and API rates
facts: Many quotas are soft and can be raised on request; some are hard limits that cannot be changed.
myths: Quotas are global — most are per-Region as well as per-account.

concepts.name: Loose coupling
concepts.purpose: means components communicate through a queue, topic or load balancer rather than calling each other directly
facts: Decoupling with SQS or SNS lets one component fail or slow down without taking the rest of the system with it.
myths: Decoupling always improves latency — it improves resilience and scalability, often at the cost of added latency.

concepts.name: Stateless application design
concepts.purpose: keeps session data outside the application server so any instance can serve any request
facts: Storing session state in DynamoDB or ElastiCache is what allows instances to be added and removed freely.
myths: Sticky sessions solve statelessness — they work around it and undermine even load distribution and instance replacement.

concepts.name: Caching strategy
concepts.purpose: stores frequently read data closer to the consumer to cut latency, load and cost
facts: Caching happens at several layers: CloudFront at the edge, ElastiCache in front of a database, and DAX in front of DynamoDB.
myths: Caching everything is always a win — stale data and cache invalidation costs are real design problems.

concepts.name: Capital versus operating expenditure
concepts.purpose: contrasts buying assets up front with paying for consumption
facts: Cloud converts up-front capital expenditure on hardware into variable operating expenditure billed on usage.
myths: Reserved Instances are a capital expense — they are still operating expense, just committed.

concepts.name: Total cost of ownership
concepts.purpose: accounts for every cost of running a workload, not just the visible server price
facts: A fair on-premises comparison must include power, cooling, floor space, hardware refresh and the staff who run it.
myths: Comparing an EC2 bill to a server's purchase price is a valid TCO comparison — it ignores the majority of on-premises costs.
